2.text: I must again repeat that the animal “spirits” produce their own charac-

3.text: teristic sounds. The walrus and the bear roar, the reindeer snorts, the wolt
3.note: Printer's error: the compositor set "wolt" where "wolf" is meant — a standalone zoom of the last letter shows a plain stem with a top serif and no crossbar, i.e. a t-shape, not an f. Keyed as printed per §2.14.

4.text: howls, the fox bays, the raven caws. The last three, however, are able to

5.text: talk, but use a particular timbre of voice, and intersperse among their words,

6.text: from time to time, their peculiar cries.

7.text: In most cases the ventriloquistic performance soon takes on a dramatic

8.text: character. A number of “spirits” appear in succession. They talk to the

9.text: shaman and to one another, pick quarrels, abuse and denounce one

10.text: another. It is superfluous to add that only one voice may talk at a time,

11.text: so that even the most lively dialogue consists of a series of interpolations

12.text: following each other in succession. The talk of the “spirits” is often carried on

13.text: in strange, quite unintelligible words, such as “papire kuri muri,” etc. To make

14.text: it understood, the shaman has to call for an interpreter, who from that time

15.text: on takes part in all conversations, and also explains to the auditors the words

16.text: of the other “spirits.” Thus the shaman is supposed to be unable to under-

17.text: stand the language of the “separate spirits.”

18.text: The same idea obtains among other neighboring tribes. The most

19.text: curious case of all is that of the shamans of the Russians and the Russianized

20.text: natives of the Kolyma and the Anadyr, who know no other language than

21.text: the Russian. The “spirits,” however, even when speaking through the mouth

22.text: of the shaman, employ only the usual unintelligible gibberish mixed with

23.text: some distorted and mispronounced phrases in the Koryak, Yakut, and Yuka-

24.text: ghir languages. After a while the shaman calls for an interpreter, and at last,

25.text: after some controversy, the “spirits” send for one who can speak Russian and

26.text: who translates the orders of the “spirits.”

27.text: The Chukchee shamans have no special language of their own, with the

28.text: exception of a few words and expressions. Thus the drum is called aˊᵋtwet

34.text: Among the northwestern branch of the Koryak, the “spirits” are said

35.text: to use a special mode of pronunciation, similar to that used by the southeastern

36.text: Koryak and the Chukchee. A few words are also said to be peculiar to them.

37.text: Among the Asiatic Eskimo the “spirits” are said to have a special language.

38.text: Many words of it were given to me by the shamans, and most of them are

39.text: analogous to the “spirit” language known to various Eskimo tribes of America,

40.text: both in Alaska and on the Atlantic side.

41.text: Tricks of various kinds break up the monotony of the performance,

42.text: which may last for several hours. The “spirits” will scratch from the outside
